content: In areas with moderate to high year-round malaria transmission, children at high risk of severe malaria can be given antimalarial medications at specific intervals to reduce the disease burden. The schedule for perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC) should be based on the age distribution of severe malaria cases, the duration of protection provided by the chosen drug, and the feasibility and cost of delivering additional PMC courses. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) has been widely used for chemoprevention in Africa, including for PMC. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) have shown effectiveness for PMC, but evidence on their safety, efficacy, adherence to multi-day regimens, and cost-effectiveness in this context is limited. Previously, PMC was recommended for infants under 12 months as intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi). New data now support the value of malaria chemoprevention in children aged 12 to 24 months. The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) remains a key platform for delivering PMC, but other delivery methods can be explored to improve access and integrate with other health interventions. Moderate to high perennial malaria transmission settings are defined as areas with Plasmodium falciparum parasite prevalence exceeding 10% or an annual parasite incidence greater than 250 per 1,000. These thresholds are indicative and not absolute for determining the applicability of PMC recommendations. In areas with seasonal malaria transmission, children at high risk of severe malaria should receive antimalarial medications during peak transmission seasons to reduce disease burden. Eligibility for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) depends on the seasonality of malaria transmission and the age groups at risk. Malaria programs should assess the suitability of SMC based on local malaria epidemiology and available funding. Monthly cycles of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine (SP+AQ) have been widely used for SMC in African children under five years old, demonstrating efficacy, safety, tolerability, availability, and affordability. For school-aged children (5–15 years) in malaria-endemic areas with moderate to high transmission, intermittent preventive treatment (IPTsc) can be considered to reduce disease burden. The burden of malaria and the benefits of IPTsc may vary across this age range, but evidence is limited. National malaria programs may introduce IPTsc if resources allow, without compromising interventions for younger children who bear the highest burden of severe disease. Schools may serve as a cost-effective delivery channel, but seasonal variations in malaria transmission and school terms, as well as equity concerns, may necessitate alternative delivery methods. Firstand second-line malaria treatments should not be used for IPTsc if safe and effective alternatives are available. The dosing schedule for IPTsc should align with local malaria epidemiology and provide protection during periods of highest risk. Children admitted to hospitals with severe anemia in moderate to high malaria transmission settings can receive post-discharge malaria chemoprevention (PDMC) with a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medicine at predetermined intervals to reduce readmissions and mortality. PDMC should be tailored to the duration of protection provided by the selected antimalarial and the feasibility and affordability of delivering additional courses. PDMC is recommended for children following admission with severe anemia not caused by blood loss due to trauma, surgery, malignancy, or bleeding disorders. Mass drug administration (MDA) with antimalarial medicines can be used in areas with moderate to high P. falciparum transmission to achieve short-term reductions in disease burden. However, the effect of MDA wanes within 1–3 months, so it should be part of a comprehensive malaria control program that includes effective case management and prevention tools. MDA should target moderate to high transmission settings and be implemented based on the desired impact, endemicity level, and available resources. In emergency settings with health service disruptions, MDA can provide short-term reductions in malaria burden, but its impact varies depending on the type of emergency, health service disruption, transmission intensity, drug choice, and delivery method. In areas with very low to low P. falciparum transmission, MDA can be used to reduce transmission as part of a robust malaria elimination program. This should include case-based surveillance, effective antimalarial treatment, and prevention tools to minimize the risk of resurgence after the MDA program ends. MDA should only be considered in areas with limited risk of malaria importation and sufficient resources to avoid compromising other elimination program components. Mass relapse prevention (MRP) with 8-aminoquinoline medicines alone to reduce P. vivax transmission is not recommended due to the potential for severe harm in individuals with G6PD deficiency. G6PD testing for large populations would significantly increase the complexity and cost of the intervention. In exceptional circumstances, such as small focal outbreaks of P. vivax in temperate areas, MRP may be considered, but a combination of a schizonticide and an 8-aminoquinoline is likely a better strategy. The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is recommended for preventing P. falciparum malaria in children in regions with moderate to high transmission. It should be administered in a four-dose schedule starting at five months of age. In areas with highly seasonal malaria, a five-dose seasonal strategy may be considered. The vaccine should be part of a comprehensive malaria control strategy. All suspected malaria cases should be confirmed with a parasitological test (microscopy or rapid diagnostic test) supported by a quality assurance program. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are recommended for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in children and adults. Artesunate-pyronaridine is now included as an ACT option but should be avoided in individuals with known liver disease due to its association with liver transaminitis. Pharmacovigilance should be strengthened where artesunate-pyronaridine is used. Pregnant women with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in the first trimester should be treated with artemether-lumefantrine. Other ACTs may be considered if artemether-lumefantrine is unavailable, but antifolates and ACTs containing sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine are contraindicated in the first trimester. Continued research on antimalarial safety in pregnancy is essential. Infants weighing less than 5 kg with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should receive ACTs at the same mg/kg dose as children weighing 5 kg or more. For individuals co-infected with HIV, certain ACTs should be avoided if they are receiving specific antiretroviral therapies. Travelers returning to non-endemic settings with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with an ACT. People with hyperparasitemia should be closely monitored and treated with an ACT due to their increased risk of treatment failure, severe malaria, and death. For uncomplicated malaria caused by P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi, treatment should include an ACT or chloroquine in areas with chloroquine-susceptible infections. In areas with chloroquine resistance, ACTs are recommended. G6PD status should guide the administration of primaquine to prevent relapse. A 14-day course of primaquine is recommended for preventing relapse in P. vivax or P. ovale malaria, except in pregnant women, infants under six months, and individuals with G6PD deficiency. Shorter regimens may improve adherence but are not recommended due to increased risks of adverse events. Severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours, followed by a three-day ACT course once oral medication is tolerated. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is preferred over quinine. Pre-referral treatment options include a single intramuscular dose of artesunate or, if unavailable, artemether or quinine. For children under six years, a single rectal dose of artesunate may be used if injectable options are unavailable, but rectal artesunate is not recommended for older children or adults.
